title: Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
content: Andy Burnham has said the government is "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse. The prime minister called for answers over why an offer to buy the business from its current owners, which would have protected jobs, was rejected. "This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families," Burnham told the BBC. The discount chain is teetering on the edge after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG). Burnham said: "We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn't been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case. "We stand ready to support the workforce however we can." The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the business 10 days to find a rescue deal. The move comes after managing director Barry Williams told its 12,000 staff the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales. It is understood Gordon Brothers wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds earlier said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future. Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1. A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale. Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer, which has left it on the brink of collapse. It could still be purchased out of administration in a so-called pre-pack deal, but the most likely option is for it to be broken up and for Poundland's stores to be sold off. Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year. It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz. It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets. A Gordon Brothers insider said breaking the firm up would allow creditors to recover more money, and that this process would ultimately offer the best outcome for staff. The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners. If this type of insolvency happens, it would let interested parties firm up offers. These include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interested in taking on between 200 and 250 stores. Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites. More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate. Bally Auluk, a national officer at the Usdaw shopworkers union, said this week had been "incredibly distressing" for Poundland staff. He claimed staff were having to "watch from the sidelines as a multi-billion pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract £30m from a business it bought for £1". He said Williams had "reluctantly" kicked off the administration process, to give the business time to find a rescue deal, adding that Usdaw was urging Gordon Brothers to reconsider. The uncertainty surrounding Poundland's future has left some staff fearful about the future of their jobs. Staff at Poundland's customer support centre in Walsall, some dressed as the Poundland "Pound Hound" mascot, held a protest on Thursday. One employee said they were trying to "save our jobs". There is also a split between the owners and the management running Poundland, who described the situation as "unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable". "As you all know, our sales are strong and our recovery is taking root. This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration," the chain's managing director Williams said in a message to staff this week. He revealed that Gordon Brothers had limited Poundland's access to funds which help it run its day-to-day business. "I'm disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have given instructions that restricts our access to funds that we would, in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement," he added. In the memo, seen by the BBC, Williams said the offer from Martin Property Group was a "fully funded, ready to go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we've made". Three independent directors who were appointed earlier this month to help oversee a sale resigned with immediate effect after disagreeing with Gordon Brothers' decision not to accept MPG's solvent offer.

analysis.reason: The article reports a significant economic event as the UK's discount chain, Poundland, faces collapse, which could have major consequences for its employees and customers.

title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
content: People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt. Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record. Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures. The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture". The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war. In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances. But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said. "This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice. "The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said. However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said. In response to this "painful" situation the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said. Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains "already behind us". Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis. The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households. Alongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating a slowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027. The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March. The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%. Frozen tax thresholds are also eating into people's take-home pay. However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions. While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations. The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year. Helen Miller, director of the influential think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the outlook was "depressing". "This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," she said. "No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy." There would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament, Miller added. "Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said. "Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added. Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions. Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could. He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households. Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in. But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" or the buffer that the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends. Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.

title: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
content: Google parent Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it rattled Wall Street with its last update of the year on its business operations. Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its artificial intelligence (AI) summaries on search were affecting ad revenue. Microsoft and Amazon also updated investors this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending astronomical sums of cash in an ongoing AI race. But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business. At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad. Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn. However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And for the second time in its history as a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments. By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before. Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of advertisements it was able to sell during the quarter. The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business. Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses." Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year. Amazon's stock also took a hit on Thursday after it shared results that disappointed investors. Shares of the company fell 6% in after hours stock trading. Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn. That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months. Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future. Jassy did not specify what two Amazon businesses those may be. But during a call with financial analysts he repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools. "One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true." As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added. "We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon." Wall Street reacted less enthusiastically to Microsoft's update, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday. The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers , which will further reduce the company's costs. Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn. Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago. Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors. But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI. "Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.
ranking_reason: Google's disappointing search business results and massive AI investments lead to a $500bn loss in value, sparking concerns about the ability of tech giants to maintain their core business growth while investing in AI.

analysis.reason: Google's disappointing search business results and massive AI investments lead to a $500bn loss in value, sparking concerns about the ability of tech giants to maintain their core business growth while investing in AI.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant and substantive development in the technology sector, specifically the impact of Google's AI investments on its financial performance. The $500bn loss in value and the decline in cash flow provide a clear reason for readers to care about the story.
